doc.title: Dave Rivello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Copying Brookmeyer's Clark Terry suite and getting his first lesson
summary: Rivello phones Brookmeyer, is hired to copy a suite under deadline, and arranges his first lesson.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Yeah. And Brookmeyer, that’s how I actually got to know Bob was he was writing a four movement suite for Clark Terry’s seventieth birthday. And I called Bob because his recording called “Electricity” had come out and it wasn’t available in the states. And Fred Sturm had said, “Oh here’s Bob’s number, just call him he’ll send you one. He’s a nice guy.” And I didn’t know, I thought because Mulligan and Brookmeyer — Gerry Mulligan and Brookmeyer were close, so I thought well Mulligan is known to be difficult and salty and everything else and I figured out Brookmeyer is probably the same way and I was so afraid. Finally I dialed the number and he said, “Bob Brookmeyer” and “uh hi” you know and we started talking, and I said I was trying to find his “Electricity” CD and he said, “Oh I’ll send you one.” He said, “What else do you do, besides write music?” Well actually he and Manny Albam were doing the BMI Jazz Composers Workshop in New York. And Manny knew my music from here because I was involved in some of the arranger’s holidays and all of that stuff. So Manny I guess had been telling Brookmeyer about me and that I was in Rochester. And so Bob said, “Oh Manny Albam has been telling me about you, I’d like to hear some of your music sometime.” So I said wow, okay, so it got a little easier on the phone, I wasn’t quite as afraid. And he said, “What else do you do besides a composer.” And I said, “Well I’m a copyist.” And the computer was kind of happening then. And he said, “Oh are you a hand-copyist or a computer copyist?” And I said, “Well I do both but I prefer to copy by hand.” And he just said, “Okay, I might need you sometime.” And we hung up and I thought oh Brookmeyer’s so forward thinking he probably wants it all computerized, I probably blew that one. And then two weeks later he said, “Okay I need you.” He called, “This is Brookmeyer I need you. I’ve got the seventieth birthday this week, a four movement suite for Clark Terry, I’m behind.” Because Brookmeyer was always behind. His way of saying it was “the muse slept late in his house.” So then every day there was more pages coming FedEx and

it was incredible because I mean the hand copied parts was a stack of music like this. And I hired two guys. And one or the other was always here, ‘round the clock, as I was copying, in the dining room, proofreading every page. Because the deadline was so close. Every time I finished a page I’d give it to them and they’d check it, and then finally —
Score. The score. So he was sending me the hand-written score and then —

Yes. Transposed. But every day the FedEx guy knocked on the door and there was more pages and we just kept going and going and it was crazy. And so during that time I said to Bob I would call him once in a while and say, “Oh I can’t tell, is this a D or an E or whatever it might be” because he was writing fast. I said, “I’d really like to have a lesson with you sometime.” And he said, “Oh okay” he said, “well you could come here and you could decide if you want to work with me and I’ll decide if I want to work with you.” And I figured well half of this equation was figured but if he says no, what am I going to do? Fortunately that didn’t happen. So that’s how the first lesson happened. And then it went on from there. And I stayed in contact with him pretty much up to the end, two weeks never passed without me calling him to see how he was doing, what he was working on and I kind of tried to stay in touch with him in that way. And it was just magical, and he was so giving and loving, and it was fantastic.
